overview: This three-page despatch from the American consul at Dairen reports increasing military-police surveillance of shortwave-radio sales in Japanese-controlled Manchuria. Prompted by the Ling Sheng affair and the February 26 Incident in Tokyo, the police required the local RCA Victor manager to disclose sales to dealers, apparently to identify purchases by Russians and other foreigners of uncertain status. The consul discusses the company’s concern about confidential dealer prices, the possible commercial consequences of prohibiting shortwave receivers, and the irony that the military police themselves urgently obtained a powerful receiver to hear news from Tokyo.

people.name: Ling Sheng
people.role: Manchukuo official whose affair prompted heightened police concern

subfiles.title: Despatch on military-police surveillance of shortwave-radio sales in Dairen
subfiles.from: Stuart E. Grummon, American Consul at Dairen
subfiles.to: Joseph C. Grew, American Ambassador to Japan
subfiles.about: Reports a military-police demand for information about shortwave-radio sales and considers its implications for foreigners and American radio businesses in Dairen.
subfiles.summary: The Dairen military police asked the local RCA Victor manager for a list of shortwave receivers sold to dealers, including equipment details and prices, following the Ling Sheng affair and the February 26 Incident. On the consul’s advice, the company supplied list prices rather than confidential discounted prices, and the police did not pursue the matter further. Their stated purpose was to trace purchases by Russians and other foreigners of uncertain status. Grummon warns that a prohibition would effectively eliminate American firms’ local radio business, while noting that Japanese manufacturers and broadcasters—and even the police themselves—were increasingly adopting shortwave technology.

interest: The despatch offers a compact view of how political insecurity in Japanese-controlled Manchuria translated into surveillance of consumer technology and foreign residents. It is especially useful for the history of radio, policing, American commerce, and the Russian diaspora in Dairen. The police’s urgent use of the very technology they were monitoring during the Tokyo uprising also provides a revealing example of the tension between security controls and official dependence on international communications.
